rationale: The security management process standard requires an accurate and thorough assessment of risks to ePHI and measures that reduce those risks to a reasonable and appropriate level. The Cybersecurity Risk-Management Program establishes the risk analysis method, business-impact weighting and treatment decisions that produce that assessment.

Risk analysis must be repeated as the environment changes. Cybersecurity Risk Management continuously evaluates threats, vulnerabilities and exposure across systems holding ePHI so the analysis stays current.

The sanction policy specification requires appropriate sanctions against workforce members who fail to comply with security policies. HR Policies defines the personnel consequences that support secure conduct across the employee lifecycle.

HIPAA Regulation: 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D) Information System Activity Review and 164.312(b) Audit Controls
rationale: Covered entities must regularly review records of system activity such as audit logs and access reports, and 164.312(b) requires mechanisms that record and examine activity in systems containing ePHI. Continuous Monitoring provides the automated log collection, review and alerting that satisfies both.

HIPAA Regulation: 164.308(a)(2) Assigned Security Responsibility and 164.530(a) Personnel Designations
rationale: The Security Rule requires a named security official responsible for policies and procedures, and the Privacy Rule requires a designated privacy official and a contact person for complaints. Charters & Committees formalizes those designations and the oversight structure around them.

The workforce security standard covers authorization and supervision of workforce members, workforce clearance procedures and termination procedures. Human Resources manages hiring, role changes and departures so access to ePHI is appropriate to the role and removed on exit.

HIPAA Regulation: 164.308(a)(4) Information Access Management and 164.312(a)(1) Access Control
rationale: Information access management requires authorizing and documenting access to ePHI, and the access control standard requires unique user identification, emergency access procedures, automatic logoff (164.312(a)(2)(iii)) and encryption. Identity Management ensures only authorized, authenticated and accountable entities can access ePHI under least privilege.

The authentication standard requires procedures to verify that a person or entity seeking access to ePHI is the one claimed. Identity Management governs authentication strength and credential lifecycle for human and machine identities.

The awareness and training standard requires a program for all workforce members covering security reminders, malicious software, log-in monitoring and password management. Cybersecurity Training delivers that foundational and role-based awareness.

The security incident procedures standard requires identifying and responding to suspected or known incidents, mitigating harmful effects and documenting incidents and outcomes. Incident Management ensures rapid identification, containment, analysis and recovery with documented outcomes.

Response and reporting requires the entity to respond to security incidents, mitigate their effects and document them. Incident Response: Cybersecurity coordinates the technical response across infrastructure, endpoints and third-party systems.

The contingency plan standard requires an emergency mode operation plan, applications and data criticality analysis, and testing and revision procedures. Business Continuity maintains critical services through BIA-driven strategies and manual workarounds during an emergency.

HIPAA Regulation: 164.308(a)(7)(ii)(A) Data Backup Plan and (B) Disaster Recovery Plan
rationale: The data backup plan requires retrievable exact copies of ePHI and the disaster recovery plan requires procedures to restore any loss of data. Disaster Recovery restores systems and data to defined RTO and RPO targets from tested, immutable backups.

The testing and revision specification requires periodic testing and revision of contingency plans. Tabletop Exercises (BCDR) test continuity, recovery and incident readiness through structured simulations.

The evaluation standard requires periodic technical and non-technical evaluation of how well policies and procedures meet the Security Rule in response to environmental or operational changes. Verification confirms that implemented controls operate as designed and meet policy requirements.

The evaluation may be performed internally; an independent internal assessment of control design and operating effectiveness provides the documented evaluation the standard calls for. Internal Audit: Security Audit supplies that assessment.

HIPAA Regulation: 164.308(b) Business Associate Contracts and 164.314(a) Business Associate Contracts or Other Arrangements
rationale: A covered entity may permit a business associate to handle ePHI only with satisfactory assurances in a written contract that meets 164.314(a). Third-Party Risk Management performs the due diligence and contracting that produce and track those business associate agreements.

The facility access controls standard requires limiting physical access to facilities and systems housing ePHI, including contingency operations, a facility security plan, access control and validation procedures, and maintenance records. Access Controls prevents unauthorized physical access to facilities, secure areas and media.

The workstation use standard requires policies specifying the proper functions to be performed and the manner in which they are performed on workstations that access ePHI. COC: Acceptable Use sets the rules personnel must follow for appropriate use of those systems.

The workstation security standard requires physical safeguards for all workstations that access ePHI to restrict access to authorized users. Endpoint Security hardens and monitors user devices to prevent unauthorized access and data loss.

The device and media controls standard requires policies for receipt, removal, disposal and re-use of hardware and media containing ePHI, including final disposition and removal of ePHI before re-use. Classification & Handling applies the sensitivity-based handling, sanitization and disposal protocols to that media.

The accountability specification requires a record of movements of hardware and electronic media and any person responsible for them. System Asset Management maintains the owned, classified inventory of systems and media that provides that record.

HIPAA Regulation: 164.312(a)(2)(iv) Encryption and Decryption and 164.312(e)(1) Transmission Security
rationale: The access control standard includes an addressable mechanism to encrypt and decrypt ePHI, and transmission security requires integrity controls and encryption for ePHI transmitted over electronic networks. Cryptographic Management governs the approved algorithms and key management that implement both.

HIPAA Regulation: 164.312(c)(1) Integrity and 164.312(c)(2) Mechanism to Authenticate ePHI
rationale: The integrity standard requires policies to protect ePHI from improper alteration or destruction and an electronic mechanism to corroborate that ePHI has not been altered. Cryptographic Management provides the hashing and signing controls that give data integrity and authenticity.

Covered entities must implement reasonable and appropriate policies and procedures to comply with the Security Rule and may change them as needed. Security Policies defines and maintains the enforceable information-security policies the Rule requires.

164.316(b) requires policies, procedures and required records to be documented and retained for six years from creation or last effective date. Cybersecurity Regulatory Compliance maintains the compliance record set and its retention to meet that obligation.

HIPAA Regulation: 164.402 and 164.404 Breach Definition and Notification to Individuals
rationale: The Breach Notification Rule requires a risk assessment to determine whether impermissible use or disclosure of PHI is a breach and notification to affected individuals without unreasonable delay and within 60 days. Incident Response: Privacy manages the assessment and response to personal data breaches.

HIPAA Regulation: 164.404 Notification to Individuals and 164.406 Notification to the Media
rationale: Individuals must be notified of a breach of unsecured PHI within 60 days, and breaches affecting more than 500 residents of a state require media notice. Privacy Notification Requirements notifies affected individuals per legal obligation after a verified breach.

Breaches affecting 500 or more individuals must be reported to the HHS Secretary within 60 days, and smaller breaches logged and reported annually. Regulatory Reporting meets those reporting obligations in time and content.

A business associate must notify the covered entity of a breach without unreasonable delay and within 60 days. Third-Party Risk Management writes and tracks that notification obligation in business associate agreements.

The minimum necessary standard requires covered entities to limit uses, disclosures and requests of PHI to the minimum needed for the purpose. Privacy Controls embeds data minimization and purpose limitation in systems that process personal data.

Individuals have a right to access and obtain a copy of their PHI in a designated record set within 30 days. Privacy Controls implements the data subject rights handling that locates and produces that information.

Covered entities must provide a plain-language notice of privacy practices describing uses and disclosures of PHI and individual rights. Transparency governs the approval and publication of external disclosures so they are accurate and legally sufficient.

The administrative requirements cover a privacy official, workforce training, safeguards, a complaints process, sanctions and documentation retention. The Privacy Program establishes the enterprise-wide privacy management program that houses those elements.

Workforce members must be trained on privacy policies, and the entity must maintain policies and procedures designed to comply with the Privacy Rule. Data Privacy Compliance provides the accountability and oversight that keeps the organization compliant with those requirements.
